name: Hesperidin methyl chalcone

card.summary: A citrus-derived flavonoid used in under-eye products aimed at dark circles and in oral vein-support formulas, where it is meant to support small vessels and reduce puffiness.
card.note: Published trials concern venous disease; none in the sources test it on under-eye circles.

quick.overview:
Hesperidin methyl chalcone (HMC) is a synthetic, water-soluble flavonoid made from hesperidin, a compound found in citrus fruit. In skincare it appears in eye creams marketed for dark circles and puffiness.

The idea is that dark circles are partly a vascular matter, with blood showing through thin lower-eyelid skin, so a vessel-supporting flavonoid might lighten the look. Clinical research on HMC is mostly in chronic venous disease, using the oral combination of Ruscus extract, HMC and vitamin C.
quick.how: In skincare it is a listed ingredient in eye serums and creams, usually combined with caffeine, vitamin K or vitamin C. In medicine it is part of an oral combination sold in parts of Europe and Latin America for venous symptoms.
quick.risks: Reviews of the oral combination describe it as safely used for more than 50 years in some European countries. Topical products can irritate sensitive skin.

lead: Hesperidin methyl chalcone (HMC) is a synthetic flavonoid derived from hesperidin, a flavanone glycoside found in citrus fruit.[7] Hesperidin itself is under preliminary research for biological effects, with inconclusive results on endothelial function.[7]

People meet HMC in two ways. In cosmetics it is an ingredient in products for dark circles and puffy eyes. In medicine, it is part of an oral combination with Ruscus aculeatus extract and ascorbic acid (marketed as Cyclo 3 Fort) used for chronic venous disease; a review says it has been used safely and effectively in some European countries for more than 50 years.[2]

Under-eye darkness can have several causes, including thin skin that makes underlying vessels visible, pigment, anatomy and fatigue.[8] The appearance-related idea for HMC is that supporting small blood vessels could reduce the bluish look; this is the reasoning behind the product claims, not a finding from a trial in the sources.

chain: Supports small vessels and reduces leakage
Less dark, puffy look under the eyes
angle.text: It is an ingredient in eye products aimed at the vascular side of dark circles. Its trial base is in venous disease rather than cosmetic eye studies.

paras: Used in eye creams and serums for dark circles and puffiness. Wikipedia lists vessel-related and pigment causes for under-eye darkness, and mentions caffeine, vitamin C, fillers, lasers and other approaches as options.[8]

The oral Ruscus, HMC and vitamin C combination is used to relieve symptoms of chronic venous disease and in lymphoedema; a review describes its effects on veins, microcirculation and lymphatics.[2][3]

A review reports that the combination has a venoconstrictive effect and acts on microcirculation impairment caused by venous hypertension.[2] A 2023 editorial describes HMC as an emerging compound for inflammation and pain.[4]

A meta-analysis of clinical trials of Cyclo 3 Fort in chronic venous insufficiency was published in 2003.[5] A randomised trial examined it in secondary lymphedema of the upper limb in 1996.[6] A 2023 randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial in 31 sedentary young men tested HMC 500 mg on delayed-onset muscle soreness.[1]
No trials of HMC on under-eye circles are listed in these sources.
